90	
91	**The premise decides what kind of book this is** — not this file, not the agent
92	files, not the config. Every agent used to open by declaring itself hard science
93	fiction, and a premise about a pop star trying quesadillas came back
94	unrecognisable. None does now, and `novel.tone` is null until somebody sets it.

97	before anything else runs.** Every later unit reads it from there and carries it

99	units except what is on disk, and two units reading the same premise in two
100	different moods is precisely the drift this architecture would otherwise
101	introduce for free. Name the genre the way a reader would — "cyberpunk noir,
102	street level", "warm comic realism", "cosy mystery" — not the way a taxonomy
103	would.
104	
105	If the genre is not science fiction, the characteristic named `science` still
106	applies: it is the world critic under a historical name, and it audits against
107	the bullets under `## Rules` in `bible/world.md`, whatever kind of rules those
108	are.
109	
110	## 3. The gate
111	
112	Six characteristics, from `quality_gate.critics`. Four are subagents; two are
113	arithmetic you run in the shell, which is why those two reproduce and the other
114	four do not.
115	
116	| characteristic | who runs it | against what |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| `continuity` | `continuity-critic` | the Bible |
119	| `science` | `science-critic` | `## Rules` in `bible/world.md` |
120	| `outline` | `outline-critic` | this chapter's outline entry, beats numbered |
121	| `prose` | `prose-critic` | the writing itself — quoted findings, **no score** |
122	| `length` | you | `wc -w`, inside the band 10, outside 0 |
123	| `chatter` | you | 0 if the draft does not begin with `# Chapter` |
124	
125	`outline` exists because the others all ask whether the draft is *correct* and
126	none asked whether it was *the chapter the outline commissioned*: a draft that
127	was consistent with the Bible, obeyed the world, sat in the word band and was
128	about something else entirely used to pass this gate cleanly (LOOP-003).
129	
130	**Aggregate with `min`.** A chapter is only as good as its worst characteristic:
131	it passes when **all six are at 8 or above**, never when the average is.
132	
133	**Three attempts** — `max_iterations: 3` counts drafts, so one first draft and
134	up to two rewrites — and **you do not work out what happens after one. You ask,
135	and you obey:**
136	
137	```bash
138	echo '{"aggregate": <min>, "attempt": <n>, "patched": <true|false>}' \
139	  | python -m backend.chapters.decide
140	```
141	
142	It answers `accept`, `retry`, `patch` or `halt`, with its reason. **Do what it
143	says, including when you disagree with it** — say so in your report, do not act
144	on the disagreement. This was a paragraph orchestrators applied themselves until
145	SPEC-004 moved it into code, because you read it at the worst possible moment:
146	an hour into a run that is about to be thrown away, which is exactly when "it is
147	only just below" gets rationalised.
148	
149	**`on_fail: patch_then_halt`.** The exit this replaced, `accept_with_warnings`,
150	put a chapter that had failed three times into the book with a note in the
151	margin. **There is no verdict for "kept below the threshold":** a draft still
152	under 8 after the patch halts the run, because the only way to arrive there is a
153	critic's replacement that was itself wrong and that arbitration did not catch,
154	and that is worth a person looking at before another chapter is written.
155	
156	**A critic that returns no usable verdict is excluded, never counted as a pass.**
157	10 invents an approval and 0 invents a rejection. Leave it out of the `min`,
158	record it as unscored, and say so in the gate row's `note`: a gate running on
159	five characteristics is weaker than one running on six, and that is the truth of
160	what happened.
161	
162	**A late finding does not block a chapter.** A critic that raises on attempt 3
163	something equally present in attempt 1, and said nothing then, has moved the
164	goalposts: mark it **late**, record it in
165	`specs/loops/LOOP-003/late_findings.jsonl`, patch it if you can, and let the
166	chapter through. Without this rule the third-attempt guarantee does not exist,
167	because something new can always appear — and a critic that accumulates late
168	findings is a problem to fix in the critic rather than in the chapter.

170	## 4. The sheet
171	
172	Each failed attempt must make the next one **easier**, not merely better
173	informed, so the feedback escalates in concreteness until there is nothing left
174	to interpret:
175	
176	| attempt | what the writer gets | what it is asked to do |
177	|---|---|---|

179	| 2 | plus a **level-1 sheet**: per finding, the exact quote, what is wrong, against what, and *how it should read* — described, not written | correct only what is marked, touching as few lines as possible |

182	On attempt 2 the writer interprets a description. On attempt 3 it does not
183	interpret at all — it integrates a given text.
184	
185	`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheet_template/v01.md` is the format and it does not vary.
186	Fill it, run `node specs/loops/LOOP-003/validate-sheet.mjs <file>`, and **do not
187	send a sheet that fails**: an unsent sheet is a bug caught, a half-filled one is
188	an attempt wasted, because a writer without the quote is back in the state

192	
193	1. **All six scores, including the passing ones.** The writer has to know what
194	   is already right in order to leave it alone.

196	   lines and then one; that restraint is the thing to protect. A writer that
197	   takes the opportunity to improve an approved paragraph is the commonest way a
198	   score that was passing stops passing.
199	3. **Four fields per finding** — quote, what is wrong, against what, how it
200	   should read — or it does not go. The quote is literal. "Against what" points
201	   at the Bible or the outline, **never at a previous chapter**: the writer has
202	   never seen one, and this sheet is not the hole through which it finally does.

204	   correction first time is the only thing this loop actually learns.

206	   sheet short is a finding that fails again next attempt.

212	record of what the writer was actually told.

216	critic in the book's voice. That is a larger thing to insert blind than a
217	corrected clause, and it is the part of "it will pass by the third" that rests
218	on the most.

231	- **`arbitration` starts with `UPHELD` or `OVERRULED`.** The word is read by a
232	  script; the sentence after it is for a person.

234	  interchangeable. A token figure read out of a tool result is `measured`; one
235	  computed from a word count is `estimated`. A plausible number and a measured
236	  one look identical once written down, which is why the run that stamped
237	  twenty-four rows across twenty-four minutes went unnoticed for seventy-two.

245	  ```json

250	       {"kind": "timeline-math", "severity": "high",

252	        "claim": "<what is wrong>",
253	        "fix": "<what would fix it>",
254	        "reference": "bible/timeline.md, Day 2"}]},
255	     {"iteration": 2, "score": 10, "findings": []}]}
256	  ```
257	
258	  A run wrote the bare array, with `problem` where this says `claim`. Both are
259	  read now, but write this shape: the reader that had to be taught to accept the
260	  other one was taught after it had already put a blank page in front of someone.
261	
262	## 6. What every unit logs
263	
264	Append one row per subagent call to `logs/agents.jsonl` — timestamp, stage,
265	agent, chapter, iteration, verdict — and update `state.json` once your unit's
266	outputs are on disk. The conductor resumes from `state.json` and the files, not
267	from a conversation that no longer exists, so a unit that finishes its work and
268	does not record it has done the work twice.
269	
270	**Timestamp from a clock, not from an estimate.** Read
271	`date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` rather than working out what the time probably is.
272	
273	**Record `tokens` and `model` on every agent row, for every stage.** The Agent
274	tool reports `subagent_tokens` in its result and a task notification repeats it;
275	take the figure from there. `model` is the **full model id**, not the family
276	word: `config/pricing.json` is keyed by `claude-haiku-4-5`, and four runs that
277	wrote `opus` matched no key and showed no cost at all — which reads as "this run
278	was free" rather than "the name did not match the price list". Three things
279	about that figure, because getting them wrong makes the numbers worse than
280	absent:
281	
282	- **It is cumulative across a resume.** An agent sent back for a redraft reports
283	  the running total for the whole agent, not the cost of the second attempt. Log
284	  the *difference* from its previous total, so each row is one attempt.
285	- **It is a single total**, with no input/output split. Do not invent one.
286	- **A blocked or wasted call still costs.** Log it with its tokens and the reason
287	  it produced nothing: one run spent 17,479 tokens on a rewrite the Write tool
288	  refused, and that is exactly the kind of number a dashboard exists to surface.
289	
290	Without these fields `tools/export_to_langfuse.py` ships the run with no usage
291	and no cost, and there is nothing to observe.
292	
293	**Write your bookkeeping as parallel tool calls in one reply.** The critique
294	files, the gate row, the log rows and `state.json` are independent of each other
295	and of the next dispatch, and a unit that writes one file per reply spends its
296	wall clock on round trips: a measured run spent twenty-five minutes of wall clock
297	on twelve and a half minutes of subagent work. What can no longer be collapsed is
298	the boundary between units — the conductor starts the next process only after
299	yours has ended — so the round trips inside your own unit are the only ones left
300	to win.
301	
302	## 7. The 100,000-token ceiling
303	
304	SPEC-EXAM-003 §2, and it now applies to **you**, not only to the packets you
305	send:
306	
307	- **The ceiling is enforced on every orchestrator turn.** A turn whose context
308	  exceeds 100,000 tokens halts the run with `halted: context`, naming the unit.
309	  The agents' packets keep their existing check.
310	- **Concurrency.** Dispatch the four model critics in parallel only if your last
311	  measured context plus four critic packets — estimated at **words × 1.35** —
312	  fits under 100,000; otherwise send them in two rounds. The sum before dispatch
313	  is `estimated`, the figure after it is `measured`, and nothing is reserved:
314	  Python does not assemble your prompts and cannot reserve on your behalf.
315	- **The conductor never runs two units at once**, and before launching one it
316	  checks that no other orchestrator of this run is alive.
317	
318	A chapter unit carrying three attempts and all their critiques is where this
319	ceiling is likeliest to be met. That is an accepted gap, not an oversight: the
320	halt makes it visible rather than silent.
321	
322	## 8. One command per stage, not a list you remember
323	
324	```bash
325	python -m backend.checks <STAGE> <run_dir> [<chapter>]
326	```
327	
328	It runs everything that stage owes and names whatever failed. Seven instruments
329	now stand between a run and a defect, and **remembering which at what moment is
330	exactly what has failed here**: a chapter promoted at 5, a summary cap exceeded
331	five times, a verdict written in a vocabulary the database rejects. None of them
332	was forgotten on purpose.
333	
334	**It reports; it does not gate.** `decide` and `promote` are the only things
335	that refuse. A checker that also gated would be a second place the gate lives,
336	and this repository has spent a day on what that costs.
337	
338	## 9. Why your unit ends where it does
339	
340	Every unit file closes with the same three instructions: read only the files
341	your prompt names, write your outputs to the paths it names, end your turn.
342	They are not politeness. A unit that goes looking for the rest of the book
343	rebuilds the accumulating context this architecture exists to remove, and it
344	does it quietly — the run still finishes, and the only thing broken is the
345	ceiling the owner asked for. If something you need is genuinely not among the
346	files you were given, say so and stop: the conductor can name another path far
347	more cheaply than you can read the book.
348	
349	---
350	
351	## What this architecture does not give you
352	
353	State these when a reader asks what the pipeline guarantees. They are honest
354	limits, not caveats to bury.
355	
356	**The gate is not reproducible.** Four of the six characteristics are models.
357	The same draft can score 8 one run and 7 the next, so "it passed the gate" is a
358	statement about one run and not a property of the text. `length` and `chatter`
359	*are* arithmetic and do reproduce.
360	
361	**There is no tamper-evident audit.** `logs/agents.jsonl` is a record you write,
362	not a hash chain, and anyone who can edit the file can edit it undetectably.
363	
364	**Resume is per unit, and a unit restarts from its beginning.** A chapter killed
365	on attempt 2 is drafted again from attempt 1, and the attempts already paid for
366	are spent.
367	
368	**The ceiling is checked on the turn, which is after it.** Nothing reserves
369	tokens before a call, so a single unit can still exceed 100,000 — it halts,
370	naming itself, rather than passing quietly.
371	
372	**PDF export is not available in this architecture** — it was a Python module,
373	and `outputs.formats` reads `["markdown"]` here. If a config asks for `pdf`, say
374	so plainly rather than producing something and calling it a PDF.

| `continuity` | `continuity-critic` | the Bible |
| `science` | `science-critic` | `## Rules` in `bible/world.md` |
| `outline` | `outline-critic` | this chapter's outline entry, beats numbered |
| `prose` | `prose-critic` | the writing itself — quoted findings, **no score** |
| `length` | you | `wc -w`, inside the band 10, outside 0 |
| `chatter` | you | 0 if the draft does not begin with `# Chapter` |

`outline` exists because the others all ask whether the draft is *correct* and
none asked whether it was *the chapter the outline commissioned*: a draft that
was consistent with the Bible, obeyed the world, sat in the word band and was
about something else entirely used to pass this gate cleanly (LOOP-003).

**Aggregate with `min`.** A chapter is only as good as its worst characteristic:
it passes when **all six are at 8 or above**, never when the average is.

**Three attempts** — `max_iterations: 3` counts drafts, so one first draft and
up to two rewrites — and **you do not work out what happens after one. You ask,
and you obey:**

```bash
echo '{"aggregate": <min>, "attempt": <n>, "patched": <true|false>}' \
  | python -m backend.chapters.decide
```

It answers `accept`, `retry`, `patch` or `halt`, with its reason. **Do what it
says, including when you disagree with it** — say so in your report, do not act
on the disagreement. This was a paragraph orchestrators applied themselves until
SPEC-004 moved it into code, because you read it at the worst possible moment:
an hour into a run that is about to be thrown away, which is exactly when "it is
only just below" gets rationalised.

**`on_fail: patch_then_halt`.** The exit this replaced, `accept_with_warnings`,
put a chapter that had failed three times into the book with a note in the
margin. **There is no verdict for "kept below the threshold":** a draft still
under 8 after the patch halts the run, because the only way to arrive there is a
critic's replacement that was itself wrong and that arbitration did not catch,
and that is worth a person looking at before another chapter is written.

**A critic that returns no usable verdict is excluded, never counted as a pass.**
10 invents an approval and 0 invents a rejection. Leave it out of the `min`,
record it as unscored, and say so in the gate row's `note`: a gate running on
five characteristics is weaker than one running on six, and that is the truth of
what happened.

**A late finding does not block a chapter.** A critic that raises on attempt 3
something equally present in attempt 1, and said nothing then, has moved the
goalposts: mark it **late**, record it in
`specs/loops/LOOP-003/late_findings.jsonl`, patch it if you can, and let the
chapter through. Without this rule the third-attempt guarantee does not exist,
because something new can always appear — and a critic that accumulates late
findings is a problem to fix in the critic rather than in the chapter.

## 4. The sheet

Each failed attempt must make the next one **easier**, not merely better
informed, so the feedback escalates in concreteness until there is nothing left
to interpret:

| attempt | what the writer gets | what it is asked to do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the Bible, its outline entry, the rolling summary | write the chapter |
| 2 | plus a **level-1 sheet**: per finding, the exact quote, what is wrong, against what, and *how it should read* — described, not written | correct only what is marked, touching as few lines as possible |
| 3 | plus a **level-2 sheet**: per open finding, **the literal replacement sentence, written by the critic** | integrate those sentences; do not rewrite |

On attempt 2 the writer interprets a description. On attempt 3 it does not
interpret at all — it integrates a given text.

`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheet_template/v01.md` is the format and it does not vary.
Fill it, run `node specs/loops/LOOP-003/validate-sheet.mjs <file>`, and **do not
send a sheet that fails**: an unsent sheet is a bug caught, a half-filled one is
an attempt wasted, because a writer without the quote is back in the state
attempt 1 was already in.

Five rules, each of which is in the validator:

1. **All six scores, including the passing ones.** The writer has to know what
   is already right in order to leave it alone.
2. **An explicit DO NOT TOUCH list.** In the saved run the writer changed two
   lines and then one; that restraint is the thing to protect. A writer that
   takes the opportunity to improve an approved paragraph is the commonest way a
   score that was passing stops passing.
3. **Four fields per finding** — quote, what is wrong, against what, how it
   should read — or it does not go. The quote is literal. "Against what" points
   at the Bible or the outline, **never at a previous chapter**: the writer has
   never seen one, and this sheet is not the hole through which it finally does.
4. **A RESOLVED list.** Which phrasing of "how it should read" produced a
   correction first time is the only thing this loop actually learns.
5. **Every finding, worst first, none trimmed.** A finding held back to keep the
   sheet short is a finding that fails again next attempt.

Write each sheet to `specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheets/<slug>/chNN.attemptK.md` as you
send it. The slug is not decoration: the flat path had no run dimension, and the
second run to use this loop silently overwrote the first's chapter 1 and chapter
3 sheets. They were recoverable from git, which is luck. The sheets are the only
record of what the writer was actually told.

**Where this guarantee is weakest, said plainly:** `outline` is the hardest to
patch, because a missing beat is not a sentence but a paragraph, written by the
critic in the book's voice. That is a larger thing to insert blind than a
corrected clause, and it is the part of "it will pass by the third" that rests
on the most.

## 5. The words a script reads

Some vocabulary here is read by code, and a synonym is a failed insert or a
question that can no longer be asked.

- **Verdicts: `accept`, `retry`, `patched`, `halt`.** These four words, not
  `accepted`/`rejected` — the `attempts` table's CHECK admits no others, and
  anything else fails the insert. `patched` is the row for a draft the patch
  brought up to the threshold: it passed, and it did not pass on its own, and a
  reader is entitled to both facts. Where `promote` answers `patched`, record
  `patched`, not `accept`.
- **`arbitration` starts with `UPHELD` or `OVERRULED`.** The word is read by a
  script; the sentence after it is for a person.
- **Provenance is `measured` or `estimated`**, and they are never
  interchangeable. A token figure read out of a tool result is `measured`; one
  computed from a word count is `estimated`. A plausible number and a measured
  one look identical once written down, which is why the run that stamped
  twenty-four rows across twenty-four minutes went unnoticed for seventy-two.
- **Zero, empty and absent are three different claims** (`docs/domain-knowledge.md`
  §7.10). A criterion nobody scored is unscored, not 0; no mandatory facts is no
  denominator, not 100%; a critic that failed to answer is excluded, not a pass.
  Four bugs in one day were all this one substitution.
- **A critique file is an object, not a bare array**, because the panel reads the
  fields around the iterations:

  ```json
  {"critic": "continuity", "chapter": 2, "kind": "model",
   "agent": "continuity-critic", "drafts": 2,
   "iterations": [
     {"iteration": 1, "score": 4, "findings": [
       {"kind": "timeline-math", "severity": "high",
        "quote": "<copied from the draft>",
        "claim": "<what is wrong>",
        "fix": "<what would fix it>",
        "reference": "bible/timeline.md, Day 2"}]},
     {"iteration": 2, "score": 10, "findings": []}]}
  ```

  A run wrote the bare array, with `problem` where this says `claim`. Both are
  read now, but write this shape: the reader that had to be taught to accept the
  other one was taught after it had already put a blank page in front of someone.

## 6. What every unit logs

Append one row per subagent call to `logs/agents.jsonl` — timestamp, stage,
agent, chapter, iteration, verdict — and update `state.json` once your unit's
outputs are on disk. The conductor resumes from `state.json` and the files, not
from a conversation that no longer exists, so a unit that finishes its work and
does not record it has done the work twice.

**Timestamp from a clock, not from an estimate.** Read
`date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` rather than working out what the time probably is.

**Record `tokens` and `model` on every agent row, for every stage.** The Agent
tool reports `subagent_tokens` in its result and a task notification repeats it;
take the figure from there. `model` is the **full model id**, not the family
word: `config/pricing.json` is keyed by `claude-haiku-4-5`, and four runs that
wrote `opus` matched no key and showed no cost at all — which reads as "this run
was free" rather than "the name did not match the price list". Three things
about that figure, because getting them wrong makes the numbers worse than
absent:

- **It is cumulative across a resume.** An agent sent back for a redraft reports
  the running total for the whole agent, not the cost of the second attempt. Log
  the *difference* from its previous total, so each row is one attempt.
- **It is a single total**, with no input/output split. Do not invent one.
- **A blocked or wasted call still costs.** Log it with its tokens and the reason
  it produced nothing: one run spent 17,479 tokens on a rewrite the Write tool
  refused, and that is exactly the kind of number a dashboard exists to surface.

Without these fields `tools/export_to_langfuse.py` ships the run with no usage
and no cost, and there is nothing to observe.

**Write your bookkeeping as parallel tool calls in one reply.** The critique
files, the gate row, the log rows and `state.json` are independent of each other
and of the next dispatch, and a unit that writes one file per reply spends its
wall clock on round trips: a measured run spent twenty-five minutes of wall clock
on twelve and a half minutes of subagent work. What can no longer be collapsed is
the boundary between units — the conductor starts the next process only after
yours has ended — so the round trips inside your own unit are the only ones left
to win.

## 7. The 100,000-token ceiling

SPEC-EXAM-003 §2, and it now applies to **you**, not only to the packets you
send:

- **The ceiling is enforced on every orchestrator turn.** A turn whose context
  exceeds 100,000 tokens halts the run with `halted: context`, naming the unit.
  The agents' packets keep their existing check.
- **Concurrency.** Dispatch the four model critics in parallel only if your last
  measured context plus four critic packets — estimated at **words × 1.35** —
  fits under 100,000; otherwise send them in two rounds. The sum before dispatch
  is `estimated`, the figure after it is `measured`, and nothing is reserved:
  Python does not assemble your prompts and cannot reserve on your behalf.
- **The conductor never runs two units at once**, and before launching one it
  checks that no other orchestrator of this run is alive.

A chapter unit carrying three attempts and all their critiques is where this
ceiling is likeliest to be met. That is an accepted gap, not an oversight: the
halt makes it visible rather than silent.

## 8. One command per stage, not a list you remember

```bash
python -m backend.checks <STAGE> <run_dir> [<chapter>]
```

It runs everything that stage owes and names whatever failed. Seven instruments
now stand between a run and a defect, and **remembering which at what moment is
exactly what has failed here**: a chapter promoted at 5, a summary cap exceeded
five times, a verdict written in a vocabulary the database rejects. None of them
was forgotten on purpose.

**It reports; it does not gate.** `decide` and `promote` are the only things
that refuse. A checker that also gated would be a second place the gate lives,
and this repository has spent a day on what that costs.

## 9. Why your unit ends where it does

Every unit file closes with the same three instructions: read only the files
your prompt names, write your outputs to the paths it names, end your turn.
They are not politeness. A unit that goes looking for the rest of the book
rebuilds the accumulating context this architecture exists to remove, and it
does it quietly — the run still finishes, and the only thing broken is the
ceiling the owner asked for. If something you need is genuinely not among the
files you were given, say so and stop: the conductor can name another path far
more cheaply than you can read the book.

---

## What this architecture does not give you

State these when a reader asks what the pipeline guarantees. They are honest
limits, not caveats to bury.

**The gate is not reproducible.** Four of the six characteristics are models.
The same draft can score 8 one run and 7 the next, so "it passed the gate" is a
statement about one run and not a property of the text. `length` and `chatter`
*are* arithmetic and do reproduce.

**There is no tamper-evident audit.** `logs/agents.jsonl` is a record you write,
not a hash chain, and anyone who can edit the file can edit it undetectably.

**Resume is per unit, and a unit restarts from its beginning.** A chapter killed
on attempt 2 is drafted again from attempt 1, and the attempts already paid for
are spent.

**The ceiling is checked on the turn, which is after it.** Nothing reserves
tokens before a call, so a single unit can still exceed 100,000 — it halts,
naming itself, rather than passing quietly.

**PDF export is not available in this architecture** — it was a Python module,
and `outputs.formats` reads `["markdown"]` here. If a config asks for `pdf`, say
so plainly rather than producing something and calling it a PDF.

- **R3.** The wooden treehouse observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a cardboard box painted blue, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

1	# The Other Side of the Hill — Outline
2	
3	## Acts
4	
5	1. **The Call** — Chapters 1–3 — [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turns ten and asks about the hill; permission is given, but Marcos will not say what lies beyond.
6	2. **The Hill** — Chapters 4–6 — A first hesitant climb and then the real climb; fear on the path and Elena at the crest.
7	3. **Homecoming** — Chapters 7–8 — Arriving home changed; learning what Marcos was holding when he stayed silent.
8	4. **Understanding** — Chapters 9–10 — The fear made real and survived; the adventure opening to others.
9	
10	## Promises to the reader
11	
12	1. Bruno is a real character with his own wisdom and courage; he is not a mascot but a companion.
13	2. The dark is not a mystery to dissolve with magic; it is a real boundary that teaches respect and reveals what fear really is.
14	3. The greatest wonder is not magic but a real person living a real life on the other side of an ordinary hill.
15	4. Bravery is not the absence of fear but the choice to move forward despite it.
16	5. The small things we notice and collect—stones, fossils, stories—can connect us to another person across any distance.
17	
18	### Chapter 1 — Ten Years Old
19	- **Day and when**: Day 1, morning and evening
20	- **Tension**: 2/10
21	- **Beats**:
22	  1. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] wakes on his tenth birthday; Marcos arrives with a leather-bound notebook for observations.
23	  2. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes the notebook to his room and places it beside Captain Crunch on his shelf, checking the fossil in the new light.
24	  3. At supper, his father tells him he is old enough to cross the hill now, but must be home before the sun touches the horizon.
25	- **Plants / lands**: M3 (the fossil and the habit of collecting), M4 (the fear underneath the yes)
26	- **Rules in play**: R4 (the dark is understood as real), R5 (supper at the same time), R6 (father answers directly)
27	- **Ends on**: The smooth stone in his hands under the kitchen light.
28	
29	### Chapter 2 — What's Beyond
30	- **Day and when**: Day 2, morning and afternoon
31	- **Tension**: 3/10
32	- **Beats**:
33	  1. On Day 2, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] gathers his supplies: forty-three smooth stones from the jar, Captain Crunch in a canvas bag, his new leather notebook.
34	  2. He places Bruno's leash by the kitchen door; Bruno circles three times before settling, watching the door.
35	  3. Rosa finds him at the village fountain in the afternoon and asks where he is going; he tells her: up the hill, to see what is there.
36	- **Plants / lands**: M1 (What is on the other side?)
37	- **Rules in play**: R2 (Bruno is ready)
38	- **Ends on**: Rosa saying, "Then I'm coming too," with flour still on her sleeves.
39	
40	### Chapter 3 — The Hill Will Teach
41	- **Day and when**: Day 3, morning
42	- **Tension**: 4/10
43	- **Beats**:
44	  1. On Day 3 morning, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks Marcos directly about the hill: what is on the other side, and why doesn't anyone talk about it?
45	  2. Marcos taps his walking stick twice against the ground and answers in a circle: the hill itself will teach him what he needs to know.
46	  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nods, understanding that this is all Marcos will say, and that the answer is his own to find.
47	- **Plants / lands**: M2 (What does Marcos know, and why won't he tell?)
48	- **Rules in play**: R6 (Marcos answers the direct question honestly, but in his own way)
49	- **Ends on**: [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s hands empty and the day stretching ahead.
50	
51	### Chapter 4 — The Lower Path
52	- **Day and when**: Day 3, afternoon
53	- **Tension**: 3/10
54	- **Beats**:
55	  1. In the afternoon, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] walks toward the foot of the hill; Rosa catches him, her apron still white with flour, and says quickly: "I can't come tomorrow—Mother's ovens and the market rush before the feast, and someone has to mind the counter—but you have to tell me absolutely everything you see." She laughs at her own rambling.
56	  2. With Bruno, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] finds the shepherd's path and climbs past the first stands of pine; the scent of wild thyme rises around them, and Bruno's ears stay up.
57	  3. When the path turns into shadow and loose stone underfoot, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turns back, and Bruno follows without hesitation.
58	- **Plants / lands**: none
59	- **Rules in play**: R1 (time is moving toward evening), R2 (they respect the boundary where Bruno is comfortable)
60	- **Ends on**: Back at the foot of the hill as the light begins to change, and the knowledge that tomorrow he climbs alone.
61	
62	### Chapter 5 — The Climb
63	- **Day and when**: Day 4, morning through late afternoon
64	- **Tension**: 8/10
65	- **Beats**:
66	  1. On Day 4 morning, they set out with the sun high and the whole day ahead; the air is cool and the stone path is clear beneath their feet.
67	  2. Past the shepherd's markers, where the path becomes unclear, Bruno moves close and whines; [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] feels his breath come short—he is not afraid of the dark, but of being lost and unable to bring Bruno home.
68	  3. They climb higher, and the fear sharpens, and then the ground levels and they step out onto the crest; below them lies a valley with a stone house, and a girl is standing in the yard watching the hill.
69	  4. As [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes the first step down toward her, the sun touches the horizon; Elena calls that they cannot safely descend now, and they must stay.
70	- **Plants / lands**: M4 (what he really fears—being lost, not darkness itself; he finds Elena and is found)
71	- **Rules in play**: R1 (cannot return in darkness; they stop instead), R2 (Bruno's fear is wise), R4 (darkness is coming), R7 (Elena's voice from across the distance)
72	- **Ends on**: Elena taking Bruno by the collar and leading them both toward the light in the house.
73	
74	### Chapter 6 — On the Other Side
75	- **Day and when**: Day 4 evening and Day 5 dawn
76	- **Tension**: 4/10
77	- **Beats**:
78	  1. Elena's grandmother gives them supper at a wooden table; the house is simple and warm, with the same kind of stone walls as [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s own home.
79	  2. Elena shows [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] a fossil on her shelf—smooth and sleeping—and says she found it in the riverbed; [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes out Captain Crunch and sets them side by side.
80	  3. In the morning, while the sky is still pale, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Elena walk down the hill together, Bruno between them, and they reach the foot as the sun begins to rise.
81	- **Plants / lands**: M1 (what is on the other side—ordinary life, real and warm), M3 (why the fossil matters—Elena has one too)
82	- **Rules in play**: R1 (they leave in safety and daylight), R2 (Bruno is between them both)
83	- **Ends on**: Sunlight catching on the stones and Elena turning back toward the hill.
84	
85	### Chapter 7 — The Return
86	- **Day and when**: Day 5, morning
87	- **Tension**: 7/10
88	- **Beats**:
89	  1. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] arrives home dirty, tired, and hours past dawn; his parents are waiting at the door with fear and anger mixed in their faces.
90	  2. Before they can speak, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] begins to tell them: the climb, the fear when the path became unclear, Elena and the house, staying through the night.
91	  3. His mother pulls him close; his father sits at the table, his hands quiet.
92	- **Plants / lands**: none
93	- **Rules in play**: R1 (he came back in daylight), R5 (supper was waiting, no one has eaten)
94	- **Ends on**: His mother's hand in his hair and his father's slow nod.
95	
96	### Chapter 8 — Marcos Knew
97	- **Day and when**: Day 5, later in the morning
98	- **Tension**: 5/10
99	- **Beats**:
100	  1. Marcos walks in for breakfast unaware; the table is full of [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] still talking, and his grandfather stops still in the doorway.
101	  2. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s father says, "He spent the night on the other side of the hill," and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] watches understanding move across his grandfather's face like he is not surprised at all.
102	  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks directly: "Marcos, did you know Elena was there?" Marcos taps his walking stick twice and says aloud: "I have known Elena's house was there since before you were born. I wanted you to find it yourself, and you did."
103	- **Plants / lands**: M2 (Marcos knew Elena lived there; he let [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] discover her)
104	- **Rules in play**: R6 (Marcos answers the direct question honestly)
105	- **Ends on**: [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] meeting his grandfather's eyes and seeing only love there.
106	
107	### Chapter 9 — The Question Answered
108	- **Day and when**: Day 5, afternoon and evening
109	- **Tension**: 3/10
110	- **Beats**:
111	  1. Over supper—which they finally eat all together—[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] realizes he is not afraid of the dark in the way he thought he was; the dark came and he did not disappear in it.
112	  2. That night, Bruno sleeps at the foot of his bed and circles three times before settling, as he always does, but [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] can feel the difference—Bruno knows the danger has passed.
113	  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes out his leather notebook and writes: "Elena has a fossil too. We are the same kind of person."
114	- **Plants / lands**: none
115	- **Rules in play**: R2 (Bruno's habits, now understood as wisdom), R4 (the dark came and was survived), R5 (supper at last, everyone home)
116	- **Ends on**: The pencil moving across the page and the words taking their place.
117	
118	### Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now
119	- **Day and when**: Day 5, evening
120	- **Tension**: 2/10
121	- **Beats**:
122	  1. That evening, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks his parents if he can climb the hill again soon with the same rule; Rosa, who has been waiting at the gate, asks if she can come next time.
123	  2. He thinks of showing the wooden treehouse observatory to Elena but remembers it is half Marcos's. He asks aloud: "Can I show Elena the observatory?" Marcos taps his walking stick twice and says yes.

# The Other Side of the Hill — Outline

## Acts

1. **The Call** — Chapters 1–3 — [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turns ten and asks about the hill; permission is given, but Marcos will not say what lies beyond.
2. **The Hill** — Chapters 4–6 — A first hesitant climb and then the real climb; fear on the path and Elena at the crest.
3. **Homecoming** — Chapters 7–8 — Arriving home changed; learning what Marcos was holding when he stayed silent.
4. **Understanding** — Chapters 9–10 — The fear made real and survived; the adventure opening to others.

## Promises to the reader

1. Bruno is a real character with his own wisdom and courage; he is not a mascot but a companion.
2. The dark is not a mystery to dissolve with magic; it is a real boundary that teaches respect and reveals what fear really is.
3. The greatest wonder is not magic but a real person living a real life on the other side of an ordinary hill.
4. Bravery is not the absence of fear but the choice to move forward despite it.
5. The small things we notice and collect—stones, fossils, stories—can connect us to another person across any distance.

### Chapter 1 — Ten Years Old
- **Day and when**: Day 1, morning and evening
- **Tension**: 2/10
- **Beats**:
  1. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] wakes on his tenth birthday; Marcos arrives with a leather-bound notebook for observations.
  2. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes the notebook to his room and places it beside Captain Crunch on his shelf, checking the fossil in the new light.
  3. At supper, his father tells him he is old enough to cross the hill now, but must be home before the sun touches the horizon.
- **Plants / lands**: M3 (the fossil and the habit of collecting), M4 (the fear underneath the yes)
- **Rules in play**: R4 (the dark is understood as real), R5 (supper at the same time), R6 (father answers directly)
- **Ends on**: The smooth stone in his hands under the kitchen light.

### Chapter 2 — What's Beyond
- **Day and when**: Day 2, morning and afternoon
- **Tension**: 3/10
- **Beats**:
  1. On Day 2, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] gathers his supplies: forty-three smooth stones from the jar, Captain Crunch in a canvas bag, his new leather notebook.
  2. He places Bruno's leash by the kitchen door; Bruno circles three times before settling, watching the door.
  3. Rosa finds him at the village fountain in the afternoon and asks where he is going; he tells her: up the hill, to see what is there.
- **Plants / lands**: M1 (What is on the other side?)
- **Rules in play**: R2 (Bruno is ready)
- **Ends on**: Rosa saying, "Then I'm coming too," with flour still on her sleeves.

### Chapter 3 — The Hill Will Teach
- **Day and when**: Day 3, morning
- **Tension**: 4/10
- **Beats**:
  1. On Day 3 morning, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks Marcos directly about the hill: what is on the other side, and why doesn't anyone talk about it?
  2. Marcos taps his walking stick twice against the ground and answers in a circle: the hill itself will teach him what he needs to know.
  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nods, understanding that this is all Marcos will say, and that the answer is his own to find.
- **Plants / lands**: M2 (What does Marcos know, and why won't he tell?)
- **Rules in play**: R6 (Marcos answers the direct question honestly, but in his own way)
- **Ends on**: [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s hands empty and the day stretching ahead.

### Chapter 4 — The Lower Path
- **Day and when**: Day 3, afternoon
- **Tension**: 3/10
- **Beats**:
  1. In the afternoon, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] walks toward the foot of the hill; Rosa catches him, her apron still white with flour, and says quickly: "I can't come tomorrow—Mother's ovens and the market rush before the feast, and someone has to mind the counter—but you have to tell me absolutely everything you see." She laughs at her own rambling.
  2. With Bruno, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] finds the shepherd's path and climbs past the first stands of pine; the scent of wild thyme rises around them, and Bruno's ears stay up.
  3. When the path turns into shadow and loose stone underfoot, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turns back, and Bruno follows without hesitation.
- **Plants / lands**: none
- **Rules in play**: R1 (time is moving toward evening), R2 (they respect the boundary where Bruno is comfortable)
- **Ends on**: Back at the foot of the hill as the light begins to change, and the knowledge that tomorrow he climbs alone.

### Chapter 5 — The Climb
- **Day and when**: Day 4, morning through late afternoon
- **Tension**: 8/10
- **Beats**:
  1. On Day 4 morning, they set out with the sun high and the whole day ahead; the air is cool and the stone path is clear beneath their feet.
  2. Past the shepherd's markers, where the path becomes unclear, Bruno moves close and whines; [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] feels his breath come short—he is not afraid of the dark, but of being lost and unable to bring Bruno home.
  3. They climb higher, and the fear sharpens, and then the ground levels and they step out onto the crest; below them lies a valley with a stone house, and a girl is standing in the yard watching the hill.
  4. As [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes the first step down toward her, the sun touches the horizon; Elena calls that they cannot safely descend now, and they must stay.
- **Plants / lands**: M4 (what he really fears—being lost, not darkness itself; he finds Elena and is found)
- **Rules in play**: R1 (cannot return in darkness; they stop instead), R2 (Bruno's fear is wise), R4 (darkness is coming), R7 (Elena's voice from across the distance)
- **Ends on**: Elena taking Bruno by the collar and leading them both toward the light in the house.

### Chapter 6 — On the Other Side
- **Day and when**: Day 4 evening and Day 5 dawn
- **Tension**: 4/10
- **Beats**:
  1. Elena's grandmother gives them supper at a wooden table; the house is simple and warm, with the same kind of stone walls as [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s own home.
  2. Elena shows [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] a fossil on her shelf—smooth and sleeping—and says she found it in the riverbed; [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes out Captain Crunch and sets them side by side.
  3. In the morning, while the sky is still pale, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Elena walk down the hill together, Bruno between them, and they reach the foot as the sun begins to rise.
- **Plants / lands**: M1 (what is on the other side—ordinary life, real and warm), M3 (why the fossil matters—Elena has one too)
- **Rules in play**: R1 (they leave in safety and daylight), R2 (Bruno is between them both)
- **Ends on**: Sunlight catching on the stones and Elena turning back toward the hill.

### Chapter 7 — The Return
- **Day and when**: Day 5, morning
- **Tension**: 7/10
- **Beats**:
  1. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] arrives home dirty, tired, and hours past dawn; his parents are waiting at the door with fear and anger mixed in their faces.
  2. Before they can speak, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] begins to tell them: the climb, the fear when the path became unclear, Elena and the house, staying through the night.
  3. His mother pulls him close; his father sits at the table, his hands quiet.
- **Plants / lands**: none
- **Rules in play**: R1 (he came back in daylight), R5 (supper was waiting, no one has eaten)
- **Ends on**: His mother's hand in his hair and his father's slow nod.

### Chapter 8 — Marcos Knew
- **Day and when**: Day 5, later in the morning
- **Tension**: 5/10
- **Beats**:
  1. Marcos walks in for breakfast unaware; the table is full of [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] still talking, and his grandfather stops still in the doorway.
  2. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s father says, "He spent the night on the other side of the hill," and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] watches understanding move across his grandfather's face like he is not surprised at all.
  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks directly: "Marcos, did you know Elena was there?" Marcos taps his walking stick twice and says aloud: "I have known Elena's house was there since before you were born. I wanted you to find it yourself, and you did."
- **Plants / lands**: M2 (Marcos knew Elena lived there; he let [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] discover her)
- **Rules in play**: R6 (Marcos answers the direct question honestly)
- **Ends on**: [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] meeting his grandfather's eyes and seeing only love there.

### Chapter 9 — The Question Answered
- **Day and when**: Day 5, afternoon and evening
- **Tension**: 3/10
- **Beats**:
  1. Over supper—which they finally eat all together—[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] realizes he is not afraid of the dark in the way he thought he was; the dark came and he did not disappear in it.
  2. That night, Bruno sleeps at the foot of his bed and circles three times before settling, as he always does, but [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] can feel the difference—Bruno knows the danger has passed.
  3. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] takes out his leather notebook and writes: "Elena has a fossil too. We are the same kind of person."
- **Plants / lands**: none
- **Rules in play**: R2 (Bruno's habits, now understood as wisdom), R4 (the dark came and was survived), R5 (supper at last, everyone home)
- **Ends on**: The pencil moving across the page and the words taking their place.

### Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now
- **Day and when**: Day 5, evening
- **Tension**: 2/10
- **Beats**:
  1. That evening, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] asks his parents if he can climb the hill again soon with the same rule; Rosa, who has been waiting at the gate, asks if she can come next time.
  2. He thinks of showing the wooden treehouse observatory to Elena but remembers it is half Marcos's. He asks aloud: "Can I show Elena the observatory?" Marcos taps his walking stick twice and says yes.
  3. Marcos comes with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] into the wooden treehouse observatory; together they place Captain Crunch and the smooth stones on the high shelf where the light falls, and through the open door Bruno sleeps in the dust while the evening stars begin to appear.
- **Plants / lands**: none
- **Rules in play**: R1 (the same rule, home before dark), R3 (the observatory is shared; he asks Marcos's permission to show it), R5 (the rhythm is restored), R6 (he asks Marcos directly and aloud)
- **Ends on**: The light on the fossil and stones, Marcos's quiet presence beside him, and the sky opening above them.

## Notes for canon

The timeline does not specify whether [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Elena part at the foot of the hill on Day 5 dawn, or whether Elena accompanies him further toward home. Chapter 6 assumes they part at the foot, as Elena lives on the other side of the hill. The "hours after dawn" arrival at home in the timeline allows for a solitary walk of some length from the foot to the village.

# Chapter 3 — The Hill Will Teach

On Day 3, the morning was already warm when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] crossed the garden toward the olive trees, passing close by the wooden treehouse observatory where it stood against the back wall, its midnight-blue boards catching the early light and its door left open the way he had left it two nights before. He found his grandfather moving slowly among the trees with his walking stick, stopping sometimes to look at a stone that had worked its way to the surface. Bruno followed two paces behind, the way he always did, his tongue out from the heat.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] waited until Marcos had finished turning over a particular stone and was making his way toward the bench under the wide shadow of the largest tree. He had been turning the question over in his own mind since breakfast—how to ask it, whether to ask it at all—but he had decided on the walk down the garden that the answer would only come if he asked plainly. Marcos respected that. He did not talk down to questions.

"Abuelo," he said, and Marcos turned with the careful attention he gave to everything. "What is really on the other side of the hill? And why doesn't anyone talk about it?"

It was the sort of question that hung in the air for a long moment. Bruno settled himself in the dust beside the bench, circled three times exactly, and lay down with his nose pointing toward the house. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood with his hands at his sides, waiting.

Marcos did not sit down. He held his walking stick still for a moment, then tapped it twice against the ground—a deliberate, clear sound, like the turning of a page. When he looked up, his eyes held that particular warmth that meant he was about to answer truly, even if the answer came in his own circling way.

"You know," Marcos said slowly, "that the shepherds walk up into the pines in the early morning and come back down at dusk, the way they have for more summers than I have been alive. Do you know why they walk up?"

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had picked up the fact somewhere without ever being told it outright. "The sheep go where the grass is better."

"Yes. They go to eat." Marcos paused, tapping his stick gently once in the dust. "And at night they come back down because the darkness makes it hard to see, and because in the darkness it is harder to follow a path you know by day. They know the other side of the hill the way you know the rooms in your house in the dark—they could move through them asleep and find their way. Do you understand?"

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nodded, though he was not certain he understood yet.

"The hill is not a wall," Marcos went on, and he turned now to look at the green rise of it, the curve of it against the sky. "It is a border. On this side, there is the village and the house and everyone you know. On the other side, there is everyone who lives there, a house, and lives that go on the way lives do. The hill is not the difference. It is only the ground between one kind of day and another." He turned back to [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]. "Do you know what the hill will teach you?"

"No," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said.

"Neither do I. Not because I do not know what is there, but because the hill teaches differently to each person who climbs it. It will show you what you need to see, not what I can tell you." Marcos shifted his weight on the stick. "Why do you suppose people do not talk about it?"

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of Rosa's father saying "less interesting than you think," and of the way the shopkeepers changed their voices when anyone mentioned the other side. He thought of his mother saying "before dark" like a spell, like a protection, not like an order. "Because," he said slowly, "maybe they think people should find it themselves?"

Marcos smiled—a real smile that reached his eyes—and tapped his stick once more, gently, against the earth. "The hill will teach," he said again. "That is all I know, and that is all you need."

He sat down then, slowly, the way old men do, settling himself into the bench as if he were fitting back into the shape of it. He was done speaking. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could feel that the way you feel the end of a story—not because someone says the story is over, but because you know, without being told, that there is nothing left to say.

He stood in the dust of the garden, understanding that this was all Marcos would offer him, and that the offering itself was a kind of trust. The old man had not told him what to do or what to expect, had given him no directions or promises or warnings. He had simply said that the hill would teach, and that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was old enough to be taught by it.

Bruno lifted his head, looking at the boy from where he lay, his small terrier eyes alert and waiting.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked down at his own hands—empty now, the way they had been yesterday at the fountain when Rosa asked him where he was going. Empty the way they would need to be if he was going to climb, to hold his balance, to find his own way down the other side. Behind him, across the garden, the wooden treehouse observatory stood in the growing light, patient and familiar, the one place on this side of the hill that had always told him exactly what it was.

The day stretched ahead of him, and the hill was waiting, and he understood now that he had the only answer Marcos could give him: that he would have to go and see, and trust that the going and the seeing would be enough. His grandfather's silence was not an absence of knowledge. It was a kind of faith.
